Birds. Class Aves comprises feathered, egg-laying vertebrates descended from theropod dinosaurs, representing a living lineage that survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event sixty-six million years ago. They possess hollow bones, specialized respiratory systems, high metabolic rates, and complex behaviors including flight. Birds radiated into over ten thousand species occupying nearly every terrestrial and marine ecosystem, making them the most successful amniote vertebrates alive today.

Birds are the direct evolutionary descendants of small theropod dinosaurs, having evolved feathers and powered flight during the Jurassic Period. Archaeopteryx, discovered in eighteen sixty-one, exhibits both dinosaurian traits and bird features, providing key fossil evidence for evolutionary transition. The Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction sixty-six million years ago eliminated non-avian dinosaurs but allowed birds to diversify and dominate vertebrate niches. Feathers serve multiple functions—insulation, waterproofing, display, and most critically, enabling powered flight through precisely structured flight feathers.

Birds have elevated metabolic rates fueled by efficient lungs with air sacs, requiring high food intake to maintain body temperature. They engage in complex behaviors including tool use, problem solving, abstract thought, and elaborate social hierarchies, marking birds as highly intelligent animals. Modern birds range from the five-gram bee hummingbird to the one hundred thirty-kilogram ostrich, occupying ecological roles from predators to seed dispersers to filter feeders.

Migration patterns in many bird species reflect evolutionary adaptations to seasonal resource availability, with some species traveling over forty thousand miles annually. Bird cognitive abilities include tool use, long-term memory, social learning, and metacognition. Corvids and parrots demonstrate reasoning abilities approaching some primates. These connections link birds to dinosaurs as their living descendants, to evolution and adaptive radiation, to flight as their defining adaptation, to feathers as unique integumentary structures, and to the theropod group from which they evolved.
